$comment: The open issues of the specification, one row per OI-n heading of protocol/open-issues.md, so check-data.mjs can tell when one is added or resolved. plain is the site's short reading of the problem and of the current behaviour; refs point at the issue's own heading first.

open.title: What the configuration proof must prove is not settled
open.plain: When a channel is opened, its verifier returns the peer's identity, limits, first trust anchor and endpoint manifest, and the channel stores them. The specification does not say which of these values the proof must establish from the peer ledger's committed state and which a verifier may accept as supplied. The first trust anchor cannot be checked against anything already trusted, so unless the verifier fixes it itself, it is accepted on first use and needs a check outside the protocol. For now each proof scheme decides: one checks the configuration against a ledger identity its verifier holds, the others take the starting authority from the proof itself, and channel users rely on the registrant's choice of verifier and on their own checks.

open.title: The QBFT epoch proof scheme has no configuration proof
open.plain: Opening a channel needs a proof of the peer ledger's configuration. The QBFT epoch proof scheme defines none, so there is no specified proof for opening a channel whose verifier uses it. The other two QBFT proof schemes define forms that are candidates.

open.title: Messages on a channel that cannot drain may never get a reply
open.plain: A channel paused because the peer's replies came out of order stays paused until the peer corrects them, and a channel closed from that state cannot drain until then. If the peer never corrects them, or the channel was closed because its verifier is no longer trusted, messages sent on it might never receive a reply, and a connector with messages in flight cannot be removed. Today the channel stays paused or closing indefinitely, and applications reconcile those messages outside the protocol.

open.title: Sending bundles to the peer is unpaid
open.plain: An endpoint is paid only for the bundles it submits to its own ledger; building proofs and serving bundles to the peer earns nothing. An endpoint can therefore receive without sending, and on a ledger that mostly sends, the margin on received messages might not pay for running endpoints. The only mitigation today is that endpoints prefer peers that deliver bundles to them.

open.title: How large a connector's stake must be is not yet derived
open.plain: A connector's locked stake has to cover the worst-case losses its messages can cause: on the destination, the execution cost of messages that arrive while it cannot pay; on the source, the penalties for failure replies. A stake that is too small lets a connector authorize a burst of messages that costs endpoints more than slashing recovers. Each CLPR Service enforces a configured minimum, but no method derives it from the connector's possible exposure.

open.title: QBFT epoch catch-up can stall across a validator change
open.plain: Under the QBFT epoch proof scheme a bundle carries a limited number of epoch boundary headers. When a peer's trust anchor is further behind than that, the bundle proves state at the peer ledger's latest block, and the validator set has changed by more than the quorum overlap tolerates, the verifier rejects the bundle and the trust anchor does not advance, so the peer cannot catch up. Today catch-up over several bundles succeeds only when the validators named in the last boundary header a bundle carries still reach a quorum among the signers of its block.

open.title: The protocol version is not checked when a channel opens
open.plain: Both sides of a channel must use the same protocol version, but opening a channel does not check the peer's, so a channel can be opened between CLPR Services on different versions. The mismatch shows only when the peer's first configuration update arrives and is rejected.

open.title: The hinTS with WRAPS proof scheme does not give its verification parameters
open.plain: The scheme describes the signature layout and the checks a verifier performs, but not the keys, parameters and proof layout a verifier needs, nor the full hinTS verification steps. Without them, an independent verifier for this scheme cannot be built from the specification alone.
